topic: Public Service Values, Ethics & Probity in Governance

items.title: Values & Ethics in Public Administration
items.body:
### Why values matter in public administration

**In one line**
Because public servants hold discretionary power over public money and people, their conduct must be guided by values, not rules alone — ethics supplies the *why* and law supplies the *what*.

**Why it is asked**
This is the conceptual foundation of the whole probity block; examiners expect the core value list, the problems that erode it, and the three types of accountability.

**The story**
A public servant decides who gets a licence, a benefit, a contract. That discretion can be used well or abused, so it must be anchored in **values**. Law sets the outer limit of what is allowed; ethics guides the choices law leaves open. The core civil-service values flow mainly from the **2nd ARC 4th Report, 'Ethics in Governance' (2007)** and the Nolan principles.
In practice these values face **erosion** — through politicisation, corruption, red-tapism and the politician-bureaucrat-contractor nexus — and officials meet **ethical dilemmas** where rules clash with conscience, or personal interest with public interest. Where rules are silent or in conflict, conscience and constitutional morality become the guide.

**Picture it — core civil-service values**

| Value | Meaning |
|---|---|
| Integrity | Conduct consistent with declared values; probity |
| Impartiality | Decisions on merit, without bias, fear or favour |
| Political neutrality | Serve any lawfully elected government; loyalty to the Constitution |
| Anonymity | The minister is accountable; the civil servant advises behind the scenes |
| Objectivity, dedication, compassion | Emphasised by the 2nd ARC and Nolan principles |

**Terms explained**
- **Discretionary power** — authority to choose between options; it can be misused, so it needs ethical control.
- **Red-tapism** — excessive, rigid procedure that delays decisions.
- **Anonymity** — the convention that civil servants work unseen while ministers take public responsibility.
- **Vertical / horizontal / political accountability** — answerability to citizens / to oversight bodies / to the legislature.
- **Constitutional morality** — loyalty to the Constitution's values and spirit.

**Accountability and strengthening values**
Accountability is **vertical** (to citizens, through elections, social audit and RTI), **horizontal** (to the CAG, CVC and courts) and **political** (to the legislature). Values are strengthened by value-based recruitment and training (LBSNAA, and the MCRHRD Institute in AP), codes of ethics, whistle-blower protection, leadership by example and citizen participation.

**Don't confuse**
- **Code of ethics vs code of conduct** — values (broad) versus enforceable rules (specific).
- **Vertical vs horizontal accountability** — to citizens versus to oversight institutions.

**Remember it**
'Law = the floor, values = the guide; accountability runs up (citizens), across (watchdogs) and sideways to the legislature.'

**TL;DR**
- Core values: integrity, impartiality, political neutrality, anonymity, objectivity, compassion.
- Political neutrality = loyalty to the Constitution and any elected government, not a party.
- Main problems: politicisation, corruption, red-tapism, value erosion.
- Accountability is vertical (citizens), horizontal (watchdogs) and political (legislature); strengthened by training, codes and whistle-blower protection.
keyPoints: Core values: integrity, impartiality, political neutrality, anonymity, objectivity and compassion.
Political neutrality = loyalty to the Constitution and to any elected government, not to a party.
Main problems: politicisation, corruption, red-tapism, value erosion.
Sources of ethical guidance: laws/rules/regulations (outer limit) + conscience (inner guide).
Accountability is vertical (citizens), horizontal (audit bodies) and political (legislature).
Moral values are strengthened through training, codes of ethics and whistle-blower protection.

items.title: Ethics in International Relations, Funding & Corporate Governance
items.body:
### Ethics beyond the state — international relations, funding and companies

**In one line**
Ethics also applies between nations (honouring treaties and sovereignty), to the money that flows across borders (aid and NGO funding), and inside companies (corporate governance that protects all stakeholders).

**Why it is asked**
This block ties ethics to current-affairs anchors — FCRA, PMLA, the Companies Act and corporate scandals — that recur in both MCQs and essays.

**The story — international relations**
States are expected to honour **treaties (pacta sunt servanda, 'agreements must be kept')**, respect **sovereignty and non-interference**, and settle disputes peacefully. There is a constant tension between pursuing **national interest (realism)** and upholding **universal moral values (idealism)** — for instance, raising human-rights concerns against a strategic partner. India's tradition offers ethical anchors: **Panchsheel** (five principles of peaceful coexistence), non-alignment and 'Vasudhaiva Kutumbakam' ('the world is one family').

**The story — funding**
Foreign aid can carry **conditionalities** that limit a country's autonomy, raising sovereignty questions. The **Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010 (FCRA)** regulates foreign contributions to associations and NGOs, while the **Prevention of Money-Laundering Act, 2002 (PMLA)** targets laundering. Concerns include opaque political funding, foreign influence and misuse of charitable funds.

**The story — corporate governance**
**Corporate governance** is the system of rules, practices and processes by which a company is directed and controlled, balancing the interests of **all stakeholders**, not just shareholders. Its pillars are transparency, accountability, fairness and responsibility.

**Picture it — pillars of corporate governance**

| Pillar | What it demands |
|---|---|
| Transparency | Open, truthful disclosure |
| Accountability | Answerability for decisions |
| Fairness | Equal treatment of stakeholders |
| Responsibility | Compliance and ethical conduct |

**Terms explained**
- **Pacta sunt servanda** — the principle that treaties must be kept.
- **Realism vs idealism** — pursuing self-interest versus upholding universal values in foreign policy.
- **Conditionality** — strings attached to aid or a loan.
- **FCRA 2010 / PMLA 2002** — laws governing foreign contributions and money-laundering.
- **Stakeholder** — anyone affected by a company: shareholders, employees, customers, society.

**Indian framework**
The Companies Act 2013 (independent directors, audit committees, CSR) and the SEBI (LODR) Regulations 2015, shaped by the Kumar Mangalam Birla, Narayana Murthy and Kotak committees; the Satyam scam showed how weak governance harms investors and public trust.

**Don't confuse**
- **FCRA vs PMLA** — FCRA regulates foreign contributions to NGOs; PMLA tackles laundering of crime proceeds.
- **Shareholders vs stakeholders** — good governance serves all stakeholders, a wider group than shareholders alone.

**Remember it**
'Nations keep treaties, funds need transparency, companies serve all stakeholders.'

**TL;DR**
- International ethics: honour treaties, respect sovereignty, settle peacefully; realism versus idealism.
- FCRA 2010 regulates foreign NGO funding; PMLA 2002 tackles money-laundering.
- Corporate governance balances all stakeholders; pillars are transparency, accountability, fairness, responsibility.
- Indian framework: Companies Act 2013 and SEBI (LODR) 2015; Birla, Murthy and Kotak committees.
keyPoints: International ethics: honour treaties, respect sovereignty, peaceful dispute settlement; realism vs idealism.
FCRA 2010 regulates foreign contributions to NGOs; PMLA 2002 tackles money laundering.
Foreign aid conditionalities can raise sovereignty/ethical concerns.
Corporate governance balances the interests of all stakeholders, not just shareholders.
Pillars of corporate governance: transparency, accountability, fairness, responsibility.
Indian framework: Companies Act 2013 + SEBI (LODR) 2015; Birla, Murthy and Kotak committees.

items.title: Probity in Governance — Concept, Philosophy & Nolan Principles
items.body:
### Probity, its philosophy, and the Nolan principles

**In one line**
Probity means proven integrity and honesty in public affairs — treating public office as a trust held for the people — and the Nolan principles spell out the standards it demands.

**Why it is asked**
'Public office as a public trust', Gandhi's seven social sins, the Nolan list and the 2nd ARC chair are all directly quotable facts examiners reward.

**The story**
**Probity** is proven **integrity, uprightness and honesty** in conducting public affairs. It goes beyond mere legality to ethical rightness, resting on the idea that **public office is a public trust** — authority is held for the people, not for private gain. Indian thought adds *dharma* (righteousness) and *nishkama karma* (selfless duty), and **Gandhi's seven social sins** warn against wealth without work, commerce without morality, politics without principles, and so on. In the modern era, the UK's **Nolan Committee (1994-95)** codified seven principles that now guide public life worldwide, and India's **2nd ARC 4th Report (2007)** translated them into Indian recommendations.

**Picture it — Nolan's Seven Principles of Public Life**

| Number | Principle | Essence |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Selflessness | Act solely in the public interest |
| 2 | Integrity | Avoid obligations that could influence decisions |
| 3 | Objectivity | Decide impartially, on merit and evidence |
| 4 | Accountability | Submit to scrutiny |
| 5 | Openness | Act transparently |
| 6 | Honesty | Be truthful |
| 7 | Leadership | Promote and exemplify these principles |

**Terms explained**
- **Probity** — tested, proven integrity in handling public affairs.
- **Public office as a public trust** — the idea that power is entrusted by, and for, the people.
- **Nishkama karma** — acting out of duty without craving the reward.
- **Seven social sins** — Gandhi's list of value failures: politics without principles; wealth without work; commerce without morality; pleasure without conscience; education without character; science without humanity; worship without sacrifice.

**2nd ARC 4th Report (2007)**
Chaired by **M. Veerappa Moily**, it recommended a Code of Ethics for ministers, legislators and civil servants; strengthening the CVC and Lokpal; whistle-blower protection; partial state funding of elections; and reducing discretion to curb corruption.

**Don't confuse**
- **Probity vs integrity** — integrity is the inner quality; probity is proven integrity demonstrated in public affairs.
- **Nolan (UK) vs 2nd ARC (India)** — Nolan framed the seven principles; the 2nd ARC adapted the agenda for India.

**Remember it**
Nolan's seven = 'SI-OA-OHL' (Selflessness, Integrity, Objectivity, Accountability, Openness, Honesty, Leadership).

**TL;DR**
- Probity = integrity and uprightness in public affairs; office is a public trust.
- Philosophy: trusteeship, dharma, and Gandhi's seven social sins.
- Nolan's seven: selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty, leadership (UK, 1994-95).
- 2nd ARC 4th Report (2007), chaired by Veerappa Moily, recommended codes of ethics, whistle-blower protection and reduced discretion.
keyPoints: Probity = integrity and uprightness in public affairs; public office is a public trust.
Philosophical basis: trusteeship, dharma/righteousness, and Gandhi's seven social sins.
Nolan's seven principles: selflessness, integrity, objectivity, accountability, openness, honesty, leadership.
Nolan principles were framed by the UK Committee on Standards in Public Life (1994-95).
2nd ARC 4th Report 'Ethics in Governance' (2007) was chaired by Veerappa Moily.
It recommended codes of ethics, whistle-blower protection and reduced discretion.
items.source: 2nd ARC 4th Report (2007); UK Committee on Standards in Public Life

items.title: Transparency, Information Sharing & the RTI Act, 2005
items.body:
### Transparency and the Right to Information Act, 2005

**In one line**
Transparency deters corruption by exposing decisions to public view, and the Right to Information (RTI) Act 2005 gives every citizen a legal tool to demand that information from the government.

**Why it is asked**
The timelines (30 days; 48 hours), the key sections (4 and 8), the appellate ladder and the controversial 2019 amendment are precise, high-yield facts.

**The story**
Secrecy is the natural ally of malpractice, so **information sharing and transparency** are core probity tools. The **RTI Act 2005** replaced the weaker Freedom of Information Act 2002 and flows from **Article 19(1)(a)** (freedom of speech) and **Article 21**. Any citizen may seek information from a **'public authority'** and must get a reply within **30 days** — or within **48 hours** where life or liberty is at stake. The Act makes officials disclose a lot on their own under **Section 4 (proactive or suo motu disclosure)**, while **Section 8** lists exemptions such as national security, cabinet papers and personal information. Requests go to **Public Information Officers (PIOs)**; appeals rise to the **First Appellate Authority** and then the **Central or State Information Commission (CIC/SIC)**. The **2019 amendment** let the Centre fix the tenure and salaries of Information Commissioners, which critics say dilutes their independence.

**Picture it — the RTI appeal ladder**

| Stage | Who decides |
|---|---|
| Request | Public Information Officer (PIO) |
| First appeal | First Appellate Authority |
| Second appeal | Central / State Information Commission (CIC/SIC) |

**Terms explained**
- **Public authority** — any body set up or substantially financed by government, which must answer RTI requests.
- **Suo motu / proactive disclosure** — information published on the authority's own initiative, without being asked (Section 4).
- **PIO** — Public Information Officer, the official who handles RTI requests.
- **CIC / SIC** — the Central and State Information Commissions, the top appeal bodies.

**Complementary measures**
Social audit (mandatory under MGNREGA), e-governance portals, open data and Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT) all raise transparency and cut leakages; the live challenge is balancing transparency with privacy and legitimate confidentiality.

**Don't confuse**
- **30 days vs 48 hours** — 30 days is the normal reply time; 48 hours applies only where life or liberty is involved.
- **Section 4 vs Section 8** — Section 4 forces proactive disclosure; Section 8 lists what is exempt.

**Remember it**
'RTI = speech right (19(1)(a)); reply in 30 days, or 48 hours if life is at stake.'

**TL;DR**
- RTI Act 2005 replaced the Freedom of Information Act 2002; rooted in Articles 19(1)(a) and 21.
- Reply within 30 days; 48 hours where life or liberty is involved.
- Section 4 = proactive disclosure; Section 8 = exemptions.
- Appeal ladder: PIO → First Appellate Authority → CIC/SIC; the 2019 amendment let the Centre fix Commissioners' tenure and salaries.
keyPoints: RTI Act 2005 replaced the Freedom of Information Act 2002; rooted in Articles 19(1)(a) and 21.
Information within 30 days; 48 hours where life or liberty is involved.
Section 4 requires proactive disclosure; Section 8 lists exemptions.
Appellate structure: PIO -> First Appellate Authority -> CIC/SIC.
The 2019 amendment let the Centre fix Information Commissioners' tenure and salaries.
Transparency must be balanced against privacy and legitimate confidentiality.

items.title: Codes of Conduct, Citizen's Charters & Use of Public Funds
items.body:
### Codes, charters and the honest use of public funds

**In one line**
A code of ethics states broad values while a code of conduct lists enforceable rules; a Citizen's Charter promises service standards to the public; and public funds must be spent with economy, efficiency and effectiveness.

**Why it is asked**
The ethics-versus-conduct distinction, the exact conduct rules (AIS 1968, AP 1964), Sevottam and the 'three Es' are frequently tested facts.

**The story**
A **code of ethics** sets out broad guiding values; a **code of conduct** turns them into specific, enforceable dos-and-don'ts. For the higher services the **All India Services (Conduct) Rules, 1968** apply to IAS, IPS and IFoS — demanding integrity, devotion to duty and political neutrality, and restricting gifts, speculation and unauthorised media contact; the **AP Civil Services (Conduct) Rules, 1964** govern state services similarly.
To improve service, a **Citizen's Charter** publicly declares service standards, timelines and grievance redress, and the **Sevottam** model assesses how well it is implemented. Charters improve work culture and responsiveness but are generally **not legally enforceable** (unlike Public Service Guarantee Acts). Finally, probity demands that **public funds**, held in trust, be spent with **economy, efficiency and effectiveness (the three Es)**.

**Picture it — code of ethics vs code of conduct**

| Aspect | Code of Ethics | Code of Conduct |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | Broad guiding values | Specific enforceable dos-and-don'ts |
| Example | 2nd ARC's proposed code of ethics | AIS (Conduct) Rules 1968 |

**Terms explained**
- **Code of ethics** — a statement of broad values to aspire to.
- **Code of conduct** — specific rules that can be enforced with penalties.
- **Citizen's Charter** — a public promise of service standards, timelines and complaint redress.
- **Sevottam** — the government model for assessing and improving Citizen's Charter and service delivery.
- **Three Es** — economy (least cost), efficiency (best output for input) and effectiveness (achieving the goal).

**Safeguards on public funds**
Budgetary controls, CAG audit, the Public Accounts Committee (PAC), outcome budgeting and social audit together guard against leakage and misuse.

**Don't confuse**
- **Ethics vs conduct code** — aspirational values versus enforceable rules.
- **Citizen's Charter vs Public Service Guarantee Act** — a charter is usually not legally enforceable; a guarantee Act is.

**Remember it**
'Ethics = values, conduct = rules; charter = promise; funds = the three Es (economy, efficiency, effectiveness).'

**TL;DR**
- Code of ethics = broad values; code of conduct = enforceable rules.
- AIS (Conduct) Rules 1968 cover IAS/IPS/IFoS; AP Civil Services (Conduct) Rules 1964 cover state services.
- Citizen's Charter declares standards and redress, assessed via Sevottam; usually not legally enforceable.
- Public funds follow the three Es; safeguarded by CAG audit, PAC and social audit.
keyPoints: Code of ethics = broad values; code of conduct = enforceable rules.
AIS (Conduct) Rules 1968 apply to IAS/IPS/IFoS; AP Civil Services (Conduct) Rules 1964 to state services.
Citizen's Charter declares service standards, timelines and grievance redress; assessed via Sevottam.
Charters are usually not legally enforceable, unlike Public Service Guarantee Acts.
Use of public funds must follow economy, efficiency and effectiveness (3 Es).
CAG audit, PAC and social audit safeguard proper utilisation of public funds.
items.source: AIS (Conduct) Rules 1968; AP Civil Services (Conduct) Rules 1964; DARPG Sevottam

items.title: Challenges of Corruption & the Anti-Corruption Architecture
items.body:
### Corruption and the institutions that fight it

**In one line**
Corruption takes many forms and hurts the poor most, and India fights it with a dedicated law (the Prevention of Corruption Act) and a set of watchdog institutions (Lokpal, Lokayukta, CVC, CBI, ACB).

**Why it is asked**
The 2018 amendment's specific changes, the Lokpal composition, and which body rests on which law are precise, high-frequency facts.

**The story**
Corruption appears as bribery, nepotism, favouritism, embezzlement, extortion, collusion and 'speed money'. It erodes trust, distorts development, hurts the poor most and undermines the rule of law. The principal anti-bribery law is the **Prevention of Corruption Act, 1988 (PC Act)**, whose cases are tried by designated **Special Judges**. The **PC (Amendment) Act, 2018** (in force **26 July 2018**) sharpened it: it made **bribe-giving a distinct offence**, introduced the concept of **'undue advantage'**, made **commercial organisations liable (Section 9)**, required **prior approval under Section 17A** before investigating an official's decisions, set a **time-bound trial** (to be concluded, as far as possible, within two years), and aligned the law with the UN Convention against Corruption. Around this law sits an institutional framework.

**Picture it — anti-corruption institutions**

| Body | Legal basis | Role |
|---|---|---|
| Lokpal | Lokpal & Lokayuktas Act, 2013 | National ombudsman; chairperson plus up to 8 members (half judicial); covers the PM with safeguards, MPs and central Group A-D |
| Lokayukta | State Acts (AP Lokayukta Act, 1983) | State-level ombudsman |
| CVC | CVC Act, 2003 (Santhanam Committee, 1964) | Apex vigilance body; superintends the CBI in PC Act cases |
| CBI | DSPE Act, 1946 | Premier investigating agency |
| AP ACB | State agency | Investigates PC Act offences in Andhra Pradesh |

**Terms explained**
- **Undue advantage** — any gratification other than legal remuneration; the 2018 Act's broad term for a bribe.
- **Section 17A** — the rule requiring prior approval before investigating an official's decisions.
- **Ombudsman** — an independent official who investigates complaints against public bodies (Lokpal at the Centre, Lokayukta in states).
- **CVC** — Central Vigilance Commission, the apex integrity watchdog.
- **ACB** — Anti-Corruption Bureau, the state investigating agency (in AP).

**Reform ideas**
The 2nd ARC urged reducing discretion, protecting whistle-blowers, ensuring transparency and speeding up prosecution.

**Don't confuse**
- **Lokpal vs Lokayukta** — Lokpal is the national ombudsman (2013 Act); Lokayukta is the state ombudsman (state Acts).
- **CVC vs CBI** — the CVC superintends; the CBI investigates.

**Remember it**
'2018 Act: bribe-giving is now a crime, undue advantage defined, Section 17A prior approval, two-year trial.'

**TL;DR**
- PC Act 1988 is the principal anti-bribery law, tried by Special Judges.
- PC (Amendment) Act 2018 made bribe-giving an offence, defined 'undue advantage', added Section 17A and a two-year trial.
- Lokpal (2013): chairperson plus up to 8 members, half judicial; covers the PM with safeguards.
- CVC is statutory (CVC Act 2003, from the Santhanam Committee 1964); AP ACB investigates PC Act cases in AP.
keyPoints: PC Act 1988 is the principal anti-bribery law; tried by Special Judges.
PC (Amendment) Act 2018 (26 July 2018) made bribe-giving a distinct offence and defined 'undue advantage'.
The 2018 amendment added Section 17A prior approval and a two-year time-bound trial.
Lokpal (2013 Act): chairperson + up to 8 members, half judicial; covers PM with safeguards, MPs and Group A-D.
CVC is statutory under the CVC Act 2003, traced to the Santhanam Committee (1964).
AP ACB investigates PC Act cases in Andhra Pradesh; Lokayukta is the state ombudsman (AP Act, 1983).
items.source: PC Act 1988 & Amendment 2018; Lokpal & Lokayuktas Act 2013; CVC Act 2003
